Exploratory Correlations

Correlations across all measures as well as key participant demographic characteristics are reported in Supplemental Materials (Section B). Of note, participants who reported more positive attitudes toward nonbinary people rated the average nonbinary person as more masculine, r(214) = .29, p < .001; attitudes were not correlated with perceived femininity, r(214) = -.02, p = .726. These correlations were reliably different from each other, z = 3.48, p < .001 (Lee & Preacher, 2013). More positive attitudes were also associated with ratings of the average nonbinary person as less aggressive, r(214) = -.39, p < .001, more dominant, r(213) = .20, p = .004, more independent, r(214) = .40, p < .001, gentler, r(214) = .43, p < .001, less emotional, r(214) = -.23, p < .001, and kinder, r(214) = .54, p < .001. Attitudes were uncorrelated with ratings of competitiveness, r(214) = -.06, p = .355, and passivity, r(214) = -.04, p = .562.

Discussion

Study 2 participants did not perceive the average nonbinary person as particularly feminine, insofar as mean perceived femininity was at the scale midpoint. However, perceived masculinity was on average fairly substantially below the scale midpoint. The distribution of perceived femininity was centered around the midpoint, whereas the distribution of perceived masculinity was shifted toward the lower half of the scale (see Figure 2). Interestingly, this pattern does not straightforwardly suggest the average nonbinary person is viewed as androgynous or gender-neutral, given the lower-than-midpoint ratings of masculinity.

This pattern may reflect the notion that masculinity is more strongly enforced than femininity (Vandello et al., 2008). Manhood is not automatically conferred to men; rather, it must be earned and upheld by enacting masculinity and avoiding femininity (Vandello et al., 2008). In contrast, womanhood is not fragile or precarious in this manner and (once conferred) it need not be continuously enacted to the same extent as manhood (Vandello & Bosson, 2013).

Accordingly, cisgender perceivers might be unlikely to attribute high levels of masculinity to nonbinary people. Indirectly supporting this interpretation, Perez-Arche and Miller (2021) found that whereas greater prejudice toward nonbinary people was associated with stronger endorsement of traditional male gender roles, endorsement of traditional female gender roles predicted lesser prejudice. However, given that the pattern of below-midpoint perceived masculinity was not specifically predicted, Study 3 sought to replicate this result in a non-student sample.

Study 2 additionally revealed that the attribution of gendered traits to the average nonbinary person did not follow the pattern observed in prior work on binary gender stereotypes.

Instead, cisgender perceivers attributed a mixture of feminine and masculine traits to the average nonbinary person, with the two most strongly attributed traits being emotional (a stereotypically feminine trait) and independent (a stereotypically masculine trait). Stereotypes of nonbinary people may thus represent a unique trait profile -people who are emotional, kind, not dominant or aggressive, yet also independent and not passive. Study 3 sought to replicate this pattern as well.

Study 3

Study 3 provided a replication of Study 2 among a sample of U.S. adults recruited from CloudResearch Connect (Hartman et al., 2023). The primary goal was to examine whether the below-midpoint ratings of masculinity of the average nonbinary person would emerge in a sample that was more diverse in terms of age, background, and geographical location than the Study 2 student sample. Study 3 additionally provided an opportunity to explore perceptions of femininity and masculinity among a subsample of participants who endorsed very negative attitudes toward nonbinary people as inferred from open-ended responses. Data and codebook are available at https://osf.io/se37b/ and measures at https://osf.io/kdw8r/.

Method

Participants

Data were collected in May 2025. Participants were recruited through CloudResearch Connect and each received a payment of $1. Participants were eligible if they had self-reported to CloudResearch that their gender was woman or man, their sexual orientation was straight/heterosexual, and they were U.S. citizens residing in the U.S. whose first language was English. Study 3 was made available to 320 participants and was accessed by 328, not all of whom completed the study. Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select 1 for demographic information). A sample of 277 yielded 80% power to detect Cohen's d = 0.17 in a one-sample ttest (two-tailed, α = .05).

Procedure and Measures

Familiarity with the term gender nonbinary (M = 3.26, SD = 0.96), perceived femininity ( = .89), perceived masculinity ( = .89), gendered trait attribution, and attitudes toward nonbinary people ( = .97, M = 4.84, SD = 1.69) were assessed as in Study 2.

The procedure was identical to Study 2 with three exceptions: Data were collected through CloudResearch Connect rather than from college students; the additional individual difference measures included in Study 2 (see Footnote 4) were not included; and just before providing demographic information, participants responded to the following open-ended question: "If you had to define gender nonbinary identity in your own words, what would you say?"

Examination of the open-ended responses suggested that most participants wrote a definition of nonbinary identity that matched how nonbinary people experience their own gender. For example, participants defined nonbinary identity as having a gender beyond the woman/man binary (e.g., "Someone that doesn't identify solely with masculine or feminine"; "someone who doesnt [sic] identify as a man or woman"), being gender-neutral (e.g., "The person has no preference and doesnt [sic] identify as any gender, they are neutral"; "People who don't identify with any gender"), being genderfluid (e.g., "Seeing oneself as being fluid on the man/woman gender identity scale, or not on it at all"; "Just fluid.

An individual who, day to day, exhibits whatever sex they feel they are"), or defying gender norms (e.g., "People that do not follow the traditional gender norms accepted by society"; "A person who doesn't conform to the social norms of man or woman and freely express [sic] how they identify"). By contrast, a subsample of participants defined nonbinary people as being mentally ill, confused about their gender, or attention-seeking. Prior work has revealed that cisgender respondents who define "transgender" by referring to confusion report distinctively negative attitudes toward transgender people (Anderson, 2023; Reiman et al., 2023). Accordingly, these definitions in Study 3 plausibly index negative attitudes toward nonbinary people. All definitions were then coded as either mentioning or not mentioning mental illness, confusion, and/or attention-seeking. Of the 277 participants, 51 (18.41%) were coded into this category. Example responses included: "I would call it a mental illness"; "a mental disability"; "Someone who is confused about their own identity so they refuse to admit what they truly are biologically"; "Confused people who are mostly attention seekers"; and "People looking for attention by rejecting their true gender."

Exploratory analyses compared these 51 participants 5 to the rest of the sample.

Results

Perceived Femininity and Masculinity

Consistent with Study 2, whereas the perceived femininity of the average nonbinary person did not differ reliably from the scale midpoint of 50 (M = 50.79, 95% CI 48.82-52.77, SD = 16.66), one-sample t(276) = 0.79, p = .428, d = 0.05, perceived masculinity was lower than 50 (M = 44.72, 95% CI 42.76-46.67, SD = 16.53), one-sample t(276) = 5.32, p < .001, d = 0.32.

Perceived femininity was higher than perceived masculinity, paired t(276) = 3.70, p < .001, dz = 0.22 (see Figure 4). Perceived femininity and masculinity were negatively correlated, r(275) = -.36, p < .001. There were no apparent order effects insofar as participants who reported perceptions of femininity first (vs. masculinity first) did not differ from each other on mean perceived femininity (Ms = 51.40 vs. 50.16), t(275) = 0.62, p = .535, d = 0.08, or masculinity (Ms = 45.22 vs. 44.19), t(275) = 0.52, p = .607, d = 0.06.

5 Compared to the rest of the Study 3 sample, this subsample of 51 participants was slightly older (Mage = 43.45 vs. 39.25), t(71.82) = 2.40, p = .019, Hedges' g = 0.38, substantially more politically conservative (M = 5.26 vs. 3.21), t(85.35) = 8.90, p < .001, Hedges' g = 1.30, and less likely to report personally knowing someone who is nonbinary (21% vs. 43%),  2 (1) = 8.28, p = .004, Cramer's V = .17. Older age, higher political conservatism, and lack of personal familiarity have been shown to predict more negative attitudes toward gender-diverse populations (e.g., Hatch et al. 2022), offering some potential insight into the views expressed by this subsample. The box elements display the 25 th , 50 th , and 75 th percentiles.

Gendered Trait Attribution

An exploratory factor analysis with maximum likelihood extraction and Oblimin rotation on trait attribution suggested three factors. The traits gentle, kind, and passive loaded on factor 1 (loadings of 1.00, .64, and .36, respectively); aggressive and emotional loaded on Factor 2 (loadings of .75 and .38, respectively); and dominant and competitive loaded on factor 3 (loadings of .59 and .46, respectively). Independent loaded on all three factors (loadings of .30, -.38, and .40). Feminine traits did not form a reliable scale ( = .46), nor did masculine traits ( = .31).

Separate one-sample t-tests compared the attribution of each trait against the scale midpoint, using a corrected  = .05 /8 = .00625 (see Table 3 and Figure 5).

Participants rated the average nonbinary person as relatively high (i.e., above the midpoint) on emotionality, independence, kindness, and gentleness and as relatively low (i.e., below the midpoint) on dominance and aggressiveness. Ratings of competitiveness and passivity did not differ from the midpoint. Thus, the pattern from Study 2 was replicated. The sole difference between the two studies involved the relative attribution of aggressiveness (lowest-rated trait in Study 2, secondlowest in Study 3) and dominance (lowest-rated trait in Study 3, second-lowest in Study 2). Exploratory Correlations

Correlations across all measures as well as key participant demographic characteristics are reported in Supplemental Materials (Section C). Participants who reported more positive attitudes toward nonbinary people rated the average nonbinary person as more masculine, r(275) = .17, p = .004, but attitudes did not correlate with perceived femininity, r(275) = .04, p = .529.

Unlike Study 2, these correlations were not significantly different from each other, z = 1.32, p = .187. More positive attitudes were also associated with ratings of the average nonbinary person as less aggressive, r(275) = -.51, p < .001, more independent, r(275) = .47, p < .001, gentler, r(275) = .46, p < .001, less emotional, r(275) = -.31, p < .001, and kinder, r(275) = .61, p < .001.

Attitudes were uncorrelated with ratings of dominance, r(275) = .04, p = .509, competitiveness, r(275) = -.03, p = .609, and passivity, r(275) = -.03, p = .672. The sole difference to Study 2 involved ratings of dominance, which were positively associated with attitudes only in Study 2.

Patterns as a Function of Participants' Spontaneous Definitions of Nonbinary Identity

Exploratory analyses repeated the tests reported above separately for the 51 participants (18.41% of the sample) who mentioned mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking when defining nonbinary identity in their own words and the remaining 226 participants (81.59% of the sample) who did not mention these themes. These analyses provided an opportunity to explore whether perceptions of the average nonbinary person differed between participants who spontaneously expressed a highly negative view of nonbinary identity and those who did not.

Table 4 reports comparisons on all measured variables between the two subsamples (using a corrected  = .05 /11 = .0045). Participants who defined nonbinary identity with reference to mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking reported substantially less positive attitudes toward nonbinary people than the rest of the sample. They also rated the average nonbinary person as more emotional, less independent, less kind, less gentle, and more aggressive.

Perceived femininity, masculinity, competitiveness, passivity, and dominance did not differ between the subsamples. Attitudes = positive attitudes toward nonbinary people. Possible range on attitudes and trait attribution: 1-7; possible range on perceived femininity and masculinity: 0-100. Means were tested for differences between participants coded as defining nonbinary identity with reference to mental illness, confusion, and/or attention-seeking versus the rest of the sample. Welch's t and Hedges' g are reported due to unequal cell sizes. After correcting for multiple comparisons,  = .0045. Perceived femininity did not differ from the scale midpoint of 50 among participants who mentioned mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking, one-sample t(50) = 0.66, p = .516, d = -0.09, or among the rest of the sample, one-sample t(225) = 1.39, p = .166, d = 0.09. Perceived masculinity was lower than 50 among participants who mentioned mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking, one-sample t(50) = 3.13, p = .003, d = -0.44, and among the rest of the sample, one-sample t(225) = 4.35, p < .001, d = -0.29.

Participants who mentioned mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking when defining nonbinary identity rated the average nonbinary person as above the scale midpoint on emotionality (t[50] = 10.28, p < .001, d = 1.44) and below the scale midpoint on dominance (t[50] = 3.20, p = .002, d = 0.45), gentleness (t[50] = 3.71, p < .001, d = 0.52), and kindness (t[50] = 3.98, p < .001, d = 0.56). Given the correction for multiple comparisons, ratings of aggressiveness (t[50] = 2.76, p = .008, d = 0.39) and independence (t[50] = 2.27, p = .014, d = 0.32) did not differ from the midpoint for this subsample. The rest of the sample rated the average nonbinary person as above the scale midpoint on independence (t[225] = 15.01, p < .001, d = 1.00), emotionality (t[225] = 14.68, p < .001, d = 0.98), kindness (t[225] = 12.77, p < .001, d = 0.85), and gentleness (t[225] = 7.73, p < .001, d = 0.51), and below the scale midpoint on dominance (t[225] = 6.44, p < .001, d = 0.43) and aggressiveness (t[225] = 7.20, p < .001, d = 0.48). Ratings of competitiveness and passivity did not differ from the scale midpoint in either subsample (ps > .14). Thus, the trait attribution pattern observed among the full samples in Studies 2-3 was replicated only among participants who did not define nonbinary identity with reference to mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking.

Discussion

Replicating Study 2, Study 3 revealed that although straight cisgender U.S. participants did not view the average nonbinary person as especially feminine, they rated the average nonbinary person as below the scale midpoint on masculinity. Studies 2-3 suggest that cisgender Americans may be reluctant to attribute masculinity to nonbinary people, potentially reflecting an overall tendency to more strongly enforce masculine (vs. feminine) gender norms (Vandello & Bosson, 2013). Study 3 also replicated the pattern of gendered trait attribution from Study 2:

The average nonbinary person was ascribed a mixture of feminine (e.g., emotional) and masculine (e.g., independent) traits.

Open-ended data revealed a subsample of Study 3 participants who spontaneously expressed a highly negative view of nonbinary identity. These participants also demonstrated a distinctively negative pattern in terms of the traits they attributed to the average nonbinary person. Nonetheless, perceptions of below-midpoint masculinity were observed among all participants in Studies 2-3. The tendency to view the average nonbinary person as relatively lower in masculinity is therefore not limited to perceivers who endorse negative opinions about nonbinary identity.

General Discussion

People tend to automatically encode others as women or men (Gallagher et al., 2025) and expect women to enact femininity and men to enact masculinity (Eagly & Wood, 2012). The present work explored how nonbinary people fit into these binary expectations. Study 1 showed no bias in cisgender U.S. perceivers' assumptions about whether the average nonbinary person is more likely to be female or male. Studies 2-3 found no tendency for cisgender U.S. perceivers to view the average nonbinary person as particularly feminine (i.e., perceived femininity was at the scale midpoint). However, Studies 2-3 indicated that cisgender perceivers appear reluctant or unlikely to ascribe even scale-midpoint levels of masculinity to the average nonbinary person (i.e., perceived masculinity was reliably below the midpoint). In Study 3, the tendency to ascribe below-midpoint levels of masculinity emerged both among participants who endorsed negative attitudes toward nonbinary identity as well as among those whose attitudes were more positive.

Accordingly, this pattern is not a mere reflection of negative attitudes.

Americans report a growing awareness of nonbinary identity (Horowitz, 2025). Indeed, the majority of Study 3 participants generated a definition of nonbinary identity that matched how many nonbinary people self-identify, indicating that cisgender Americans can describe nonbinary gender accurately. That participants nonetheless did not ascribe much masculinity to the average nonbinary person is notable. Whereas cisgender people can spontaneously express the notion that nonbinary gender may reflect a mixture of femininity and masculinity, they nonetheless tended to rate the average nonbinary person as below the scale midpoint on masculinity (and at the midpoint on femininity). Thus, for some participants, perceptions of femininity and masculinity did not entirely match their own definitions of nonbinary identity. This pattern might be associated with the generally strict enforcement of masculine gender norms (Vandello & Bosson, 2013). For example, gender norms dictate that "real men" must avoid any appearance of femininity (Vandello et al., 2008). By contrast, gender norms for women are relatively less rigid (Bosson et al., 2022; Sczesny et al., 2025). Masculinity is thus a valued characteristic that is not easily or automatically granted to men. Refraining from perceiving even at-midpoint levels of masculinity in nonbinary people might reflect this overall tendency to reserve masculinity primarily for those deemed "real men."

The pattern of relatively low masculinity and midpoint-levels of femininity attributed to the average nonbinary person may speak to prior findings that nonbinary gender is perceived as less "real" than binary gender identities (McCarty & Burt, 2024; Valen & Burke, 2025).

Perceiving gender appears to be critical to perceiving humanness, such that targets who are not assigned a specific gender are rated as less human compared to targets who are described as female or male (Martin & Mason, 2022). It is possible that nonbinary gender identity is deemed invalid or "not real" because nonbinary people are not perceived as either clearly feminine or clearly masculine. Future research might test this possibility directly.

Studies 2-3 additionally revealed that traits that are typically selectively attributed to women or men did not follow the same factor structure when participants considered how they might apply to nonbinary people. Instead, the average nonbinary person was ascribed a profile of traits consisting of both stereotypically feminine (e.g., emotional) and masculine (e.g., independent) characteristics. One possibility is that nonbinary people are viewed as akin to

LGBTQ+ rights activists. The joint attribution of traits such as emotional and independent might thus reflect characteristics that are stereotypically ascribed to activists from marginalized groups, which tend to signal strength and emotional reactivity (Burrows et al., 2022). In general, the present studies are consistent with the notion that femininity and masculinity are not the endpoints of one continuum (Hester et al., 2021). Rather, people are perceived as possessing varying levels of both femininity and masculinity.

Limitations and Future Directions

Despite providing insight into how straight cisgender Americans think about nonbinary gender, the present studies have limitations that must be considered when interpreting the findings. First, it is important to emphasize that the present work examined how straight cisgender respondents think about the overall category of nonbinary people and cannot speak to how specific nonbinary persons might be perceived. For example, perceptions of a nonbinary target person (e.g., based on a photograph or actual social interaction) as feminine or masculine are likely in part determined by the particular gender expression (e.g., appearance, clothing) of the individual being perceived. Additionally, prior work has shown that attitudes toward genderdiverse populations differ as a function of whether the social context is gender-segregated or gender-integrated. In particular, straight cisgender Americans report more negative attitudes toward transgender people when considering gender-segregated life domains such as restrooms or locker rooms, compared to gender-integrated life domains such as education and employment (Buck & Obzud, 2018). Perceptions of nonbinary people's femininity and masculinity might thus be different if respondents were considering life domains that make (binary) gender salient.

Furthermore, whereas Study 2's findings regarding perceived femininity and masculinity were replicated in Study 3, Study 1's results regarding a lack of bias in terms of assumptions about assigned sex (female vs. male) would benefit from replication. Attempts to replicate this specific finding might employ task instructions that are more succinct and thus easier to parse than the relatively wordy language used in Study 1. In general, future work ought to examine whether cisgender people possess a perceptual category of "gender nonbinary" or whether all targets are spontaneously categorized as either women or men (regardless of their actual gender identity), and how such perceptual processes relate to targets' gender expression and the contextual salience of gender.

Second, participants reported on their perceptions of the average nonbinary person in isolation, without direct comparisons to targets with binary gender identities (whether cisgender or transgender). On one hand, this design provides insight into what comes to mind most immediately when cisgender people consider the average nonbinary person, thereby perhaps illustrating parts of the prototype of the category "nonbinary people." On the other hand, asking participants to rate their perceptions of the femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people as well as women and men would provide comparative information that the present studies lack.

Future studies would do well to use within-subjects designs of this kind.

Third, specific identities that fall under the nonbinary umbrella term might result in distinct patterns of perceived femininity and masculinity. People who identify as gender-neutral, agender, genderfluid, or genderqueer are plausibly perceived differently from one another.

Additionally, nonbinary individuals who use they/them pronouns or neopronouns (e.g., fae/fem, ze/zir) may also evoke distinct patterns of gender perception and gendered trait attribution.

Future research might productively address these possibilities.

Fourth, although it is possible to speculate about the implications of how nonbinary people are perceived in terms of femininity and masculinity, the task of directly examining these consequences must be taken up in future studies. For example, are nonbinary people seen as less human, or is their gender identity invalidated, as a function of the levels of femininity and masculinity attributed to them? Under what circumstances do cisgender people view nonbinary people as more or less gendered? Answers to such questions would help elucidate how people perceive gender in general (Martin & Slepian, 2025).

Fifth, the present data came from primarily straight cisgender U.S. residents. As such, all patterns are limited to the U.S. cultural context. There is considerable cultural variation in the prevalence of genders that exist outside the binary, and it remains entirely possible that nonbinary people are perceived systematically differently across cultures. Importantly, the present samples are also not representative of the U.S. Associations between dependent measures and participant demographic characteristics are reported in Supplemental Materials and indicate that only participant gender and political conservatism consistently correlated with perceptions of the average nonbinary person (with men, relative to women, ascribing more femininity and less masculinity, and more conservative participants attributing more negative traits). Moreover, Democrats (vs. Republicans) were overrepresented in the present work. The current U.S. political landscape frequently uses gender identity as a wedge issue, and Americans' views on gender identity are strongly politically polarized (Pew Research Center, 2025). As such, the imbalance in terms of political party affiliation may complicate the interpretation of the present results, despite the presence of a subsample of participants in Study 3 who were clearly relatively conservative in terms of their views on nonbinary gender. More broadly speaking, as politics change at the societal level, so too might perceptions of nonbinary people at the individual level.

Accordingly, in addition to being limited to nonrepresentative samples of straight cisgender Democrat-leaning U.S.-based perceivers, the patterns observed here may reflect the specifics of a particular sociopolitical moment.

Conclusion

Gender identity diversity has increased in the U.S. and worldwide, especially among younger generations (Brown, 2022; Horowitz, 2025). Many cisgender perceivers nonetheless expect everyone to have a binary gender identity (Public Religion Research Institute, 2023) and to enact their gender as either clearly feminine-presenting or masculine-presenting (Martin & Slepian, 2020 , 2025). Nonbinary people explicitly defy these expectations and are thus likely to face backlash. The present work suggests that straight cisgender perceivers in the U.S. have specific assumptions about the femininity and masculinity of the average nonbinary person. A particular nonbinary individual may or may not meet these assumptions, suggesting another potential avenue for backlash to emerge. People who work with nonbinary individuals (e.g., healthcare providers, social workers, educators) should be aware of their own assumptions and the potential for bias stemming from deep-seated beliefs about the nature of gender and gendered characteristics. More broadly, understanding the ascription of femininity and masculinity to individuals who do not conform to traditional binary genders is key to ensuring gender equality.

SECTION D: Replicating Study 2 Analyses After Excluding Data from Non-Heterosexual Participants

Perceived Femininity and Masculinity Do straight cisgender respondents in Study 2 (n = 168) perceive the average nonbinary person as feminine and/or masculine? One-sample t-tests showed that whereas mean perceived femininity did not differ reliably from 50 (M = 50.84, SD = 15.36), t(167) = 0.71, p = .479, d = 0.06, mean perceived masculinity was reliably lower than 50 (M = 40.44, SD = 15.79), t(167) = 7.84, p < .001, d = 0.61. Perceived femininity was reliably higher than perceived masculinity, t(167) = 6.36, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 0.49. Perceived femininity and masculinity were uncorrelated, r(166) = .08, p = .335. Thus, the patterns reported in the main text replicated in this smaller subsample of Study 2 participants who reported being straight/heterosexual.

Gendered Trait Attribution

Do straight cisgender respondents attribute traditionally feminine and/or masculine traits to the average nonbinary person? One-sample t-tests compared the attribution of each trait against the scale midpoint (4, "neither agree nor disagree"). A corrected  = .05 /8 = .00625 was employed for these analyses. Results are reported in the table below. Straight cisgender participants in Study 2 rated the average nonbinary person as relatively high (i.e., reliably above the midpoint) on emotionality, independence, kindness, and gentleness. Ratings of competitiveness and passivity were not reliably different from the midpoint. Although ratings of dominance and aggressiveness were below the scale midpoint, these comparisons did not survive Bonferroni correction in this smaller subsample. Otherwise, all patterns reported in the main text replicated in this smaller subsample of Study 2 participants who reported being straight/heterosexual.

Exploratory Correlations

Straight cisgender Study 2 participants who reported more positive attitudes toward nonbinary people rated the average nonbinary person as more masculine, r(166) = .32, p < .001; attitudes were not correlated with perceived femininity, r(166) = -.02, p = .803. These two correlations were reliably different from each other, z = 3.33, p < .001. More positive attitudes were associated with ratings of the average nonbinary person as less aggressive, r(166) = -.43, p < .001, more dominant, r(165) = .22, p = .004, more independent, r(166) = .46, p < .001, gentler, r(166) = .47, p < .001, less emotional, r(166) = -.25, p < .001, and kinder, r(166) = .54, p < .001. Attitudes were not reliably associated with ratings of competitiveness, r(166) = -.03, p = .671, or passivity, r(166) = -.01, p = .938. Thus, the correlations reported in the main text replicated in this smaller subsample of Study 2 participants who reported being straight/heterosexual.

Study 1 was made available to 350 participants and was accessed by 371, not all of whom completed the study. Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select "slightly disagree" to an attention-check item requesting that response (n = 34); (b) their CloudResearch identification number appeared more than once in the data file, suggesting they accessed the study multiple times (n = 17); (c) their self-reported sexual orientation did not match what they had previously reported to CloudResearch (n = 5; n = 21 did not report their sexual orientation and were also excluded); (d) they provided an incoherent response to an open-ended question (n = 8; n = 21 did not respond to this question and were also excluded); or (e) their Qualtrics reCAPTCHA score was less than 0.50 (n = 1; Qualtrics generates this score automatically and scores below 0.5 indicate possible bot-generated responses according to the Qualtrics algorithm).

Unlike Studies 1 and 3, recruitment in Study 2 was not restricted to participants who identified as straight/heterosexual and the Study 2 sample is therefore more diverse in terms of sexual orientation. Given prior findings of differences in attitudes toward gender-diverse populations as a function of respondent sexual orientation (e.g.,Anderson, 2023), all analyses reported below were re-conducted after excluding data from participants who did not identify as straight/heterosexual. These analyses are reported in Supplemental Materials (Section D). With the exception of two post-hoc comparisons on trait attribution that did not survive correction for multiple comparisons in this smaller subsample, all patterns replicated.

Participants also completed measures of gender essentialism, ambivalent sexism, and gender identification. These measures are not discussed further; however, all Study 2 data are available at https://osf.io/b85s3/.
